label: text
text: Three hundred years' association is claimed by some local Chinese, householders who were revicted by the Police yesterday after a long series of incidents starting from a deluge of a few wet seasons ago.

label: text
text: Early in the morning, divisional Inspector J. Ogg, of Wanchat station, took a posse comprising a European sergeant and ten Indians and Chinese down to Wong-nei-chong village. With the officers were representatives of the Public Works Department, for which several gangs of cookies had assembled to do the manual part of the job.

label: text
text: Verbal notice had been given on Saturday that the houses were to be demolished. As is characteristic of the Chinese masses, the inhabitants of the village delayed things till the very last minute. When the Police arrived they took matters stoically—after having hoped against hope for months on end, that they would be allowed to stay in tenements which nature had made both dangerous and insignificantly.

label: text
text: There was no "fun" similar to that when the Sheriff's officer went to evict the Clydebank workers who refused to pay rent. The only incident was when two women disputed ownership of a small board that was only worth a few cents. Knick-knacks and sundries that the foreigner was positive nobody could have any earthly use for were carried away with precision.

label: text
text: Each house was of only one floor and three ordinary office desks would have filled up the floor space up to the roof. The removal was a matter of only an hour or so and then the "pioneers" set to work with picks and shovels.

label: text
text: When the race-course was "mudded" a few years ago, the village was flooded out and a number of the hovels collapsed. With the deluges repeated, the place was deemed dangerous. Water stood several feet deep in the narrow lanes, and earth was piled up everywhere.

label: text
text: Negotiations are proceeding between the Government and respective owners for an interchange of lots. During the last months, a number of the small owners have been paid at Government expense to live away from their homes.

label: text
text: Yesterday the real work of pulling the village down began and modern houses will, it is hoped spring up very soon.

label: text
text: A number of the inhabitants are very hazy as to the conditions and they are afraid that they may be (in their opinion) unfairly treated. Their one obsession is to retain their present lots, but no one seems to be clear how he is going to keep the rickety house standing, or what he is going to live in. The Government has made a promise and a solution must come in time.

label: text
text: These people are of a clan which migrated to Hongkong long before it was seeded to Britain. Some have been there for not less than seven generations, whilst others maintain that their family has lived there for three hundred years.

label: text
text: In the property boom of three years back, a number were tempted to sell their “heirlooms.” But they did not leave the place. They went a little higher up the hill, “marked out a claim” on Crown land, put up matsheds, and are still living there to-day.

label: text
text: Imprisonment without the option of a fine was meted out to offenders at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning in further thefts of rice.

label: text
text:
Three women pleaded guilty to theft of 218 lbs. rice from the s.s. "Kwongtung" and were each given two months' hard labour.
A boatman and a woman who were charged with receiving the rice, knowing same to have been stolen, admitted in answer to a question that they knew the rice was swept from the decks of the vessel. The man, having previous conviction, was sentenced to four months' hard labour and the woman to two months.

label: text
text: That a petition is to be prepared for presentation to the Government was the decision arrived at by the general meeting of the Hongkong Tenants' Protective Association.

label: text
text: Reasons advanced for resembling the Rents Restriction Ordinance (in the speakers' opinion): All effects of restrictions on owners of property; the increase of 15 per cent. on standard events (sanctioned last year) not being high enough in ratio to the rise in other costs of living; the number of vacant tenements in the Colony.

label: text
text: Arguments against the rescinding of the Ordinance were advanced, as follows: If no restriction is placed on the power to increase rentals, rents will be put up to such an extent that other costs will have to go up in proportion, thereby, tending to a high rate of living, demands for increased wages, etc., the statement that "if rents of restricted houses (i.e., those coming within the Ordinance) are put up, tenants can move" to houses at present vacant, is not true in fact, as the question of situation is of paramount importance to business, shops etc., bona fide landlords do not favour exploitation in rents, for which speculators and subsidiary landlords (i.e., "principal tenants") are responsible; the number of vacant tenements in the Colony, at present is not due to the presence of the Ordinance, but to the crisis.

label: text
text: As has been stated, the meeting was convened to discuss a proposal to petition the Government to continue the Ordinance (after June 30, 1926) or maintain some form of limited restriction.

label: text
text: Dr. C. C. Wu, the Mayor of Canton, who is reported to be likely to visit the Colony this week, did not arrive yesterday.

label: text
text: Up till tiffin time to-day there had been, as far as is known, no official intimation that he was coming down by the Steamboat Co.'s steamer this afternoon.

label: text
text: Vernacular papers indicate that if Dr. Wu does come down, his visit may only be in the nature of a complimentary return call to the Hon. Mr. J. H. Kemp (Attorney-General) who went up to Canton some days ago and entered into unofficial conversations with Dr. Wu, relative to the projected conference to end the boycott.

label: text
text: What appears to be a bomb was found on Saturday when the police entered the ground floor of No. 24, Yee Wo Street, Causeway Bay, in consequence of which three Chinese were arrested.

label: text
text: Sub-Inspector Field brought the men before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning and asked for three days' formal remand. The accused were accordingly remanded in police custody until Friday morning

label: text
text: Pleading guilty at the Central Magistracy, this morning to a charge of falling to produce his motor driver's licence when asked to do so by a traffic officer, Mr. F. Baker, of the P.W.D., was fined $6.

label: text
text: Two hales of raw silk, valued at $440, are reported to have been stolen from a truck left unattended at Ko Shing Street yesterday. Another report made by a Chinese woman states that $240 worth of jewellery was stolen from a safe in her house at Quen's Road West.

label: text
text: The death is announced of Lady Blake, widow of the late Sir Henry Arthur Blake, G.C.M.G., K.C.M.G., C.M.G., F.R.G.S., (ex-Governor of Hongkong) at Youghal, Ireland.

label: text
text: Lady Blake was in Hongkong during the five years (1898-1903) in which the late Sir Henry Blake was Governor and in which period the New Territories were taken over from the Chinese (April 1899.)

label: text
text: . Lady Blake was the daughter of Bernal Osbourn, a well-known politician of the mid-Victorian period and the late Sir Henry Blake, who was a popular and able administrator, admitted that he owed much of his success in life to the advice and ability of Lady Blake.

label: text
text: Lady Blake took a keen interest in the movement organised to abolish the compulsory binding of women's feet in China and Sir Henry Pollock, K.C., who was Attorney-General during the late Sir Henry's administration, recalls a meeting in Hongkong, addressed by Mrs. Archibald Little, a moving spirit in the organisation, over which Lady Blake presided.

label: text
text: Lady Blake and Miss Olive Blake, their daughter, who married shortly after leaving Hongkong, accompanied the late Sir Henry to Ceylon where he was Governor for a short time; on his retirement in 1907 and since his death, Lady Blake has lived at the late Sir Henry's home at Youghal, Ireland.

label: text
text: The late Sir Henry Blake commenced his public career in Ireland, having been a resident magistrate and one of the five special resident magistrates selected by the Government to concert and carry out measures for the pacification of a large portion of Ireland.

label: text
text: Prior to coming to Hongkong, the late Sir Henry Blake had been Governor of the Bahamas and of Jamaica.

label: text
text: A report made by the master of a junk which returned to the Colony on Sunday gives details of a piracy in Chinese waters on April 8 while on a voyage to Amoy with a cargo of kerosene and matches.

label: text
text: About 18 men set off from the shore near Sze Ling in Chinese territory and, bringing their boat alongside the junk, clambered aboard. Brandishing revolvers, they drove the crew into the forehold and closed the hatch on them. One member of the crew who attempted to lift the hatch cover to see what the pirates were doing was shot in the elbow.

label: text
text: The men were imprisoned for seven days and the only food which the pirates gave them was one meal a day. Hearing no noise on board on the last day of their imprisonment, the crew scrambled out and found the pirates had gone, having taken them cargo to the value of $1,724.

label: text
text: The junk made for Samun where a report of the occurrence was made to the Customs authorities and then steered for Hongkong. The Water Police were notified on arrival and had the injured man sent to the Kwong Wah Hospital.

label: text
text:
A coolle employed by Messrs. Trollope and Colls was sentenced at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning to undergo one month's imprisonment for theft of 15 empty sacks from the Peninsula Hotel.
While Professor M. A. Simpson was driving his car along Bonham Road yesterday, a Chinese boy suddenly crossed the road and was struck down. The boy was cut in the lips and was detained at the Government Civil Hospital.

label: text
text: That he merely hid the sum of $10,600 in notes, for a joke on the owner, was the excuse alleged to have been offered by a Chinese who has been taken into custody in connection with the disappearance of that sum from a resident at the Great Eastern Hotel, Connaught Road Central, last Friday.

label: text
text:
The loss was reported
Saturday's "China Mail"

label: text
text:
Saturday's China Man.
On the Police being communicated with, detectives set to work, and a friend of the "victim" was detained.

label: text
text: Subsequently he is said to have admitted taking the money, merely for fun and with no ulterior motive. Accompanied by police and the owner, he led the way to premises in the western district which were used as the office of a pig loan (i.e., a wholesale pig depot).

label: text
text: His uncle gave the man a very good character. The uncle is stated to have explained that when he was asked to put the notes in the safe, he was told that they were collections by the nephew.

label: text
text: When charged before Major C. Willson at the Central Magistracy this morning with the theft of the money, accused was remanded for three days.

label: text
text: Another interesting wedding, in which the Chinese social community was particularly interested, took place at St. John's Cathedral this afternoon, the parties being Miss Elizabeth Lu-Sien Wong, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. M. Wong; and Mr. S. B. Tan, son of the late Mr. and Mrs. Tan Cheng-tuan, of Singapore.

label: text
text:
The Rev. H. Copley Moyl
officiated.

label: text
text: The Misses Beatrice Lam (cousin), Estelle Mayes and Josephine Wong (sister) attended the bride as bridesmaids and Masters Stephen and Enoch Wong (cousins) as pages.

label: text
text: The bridesmaids wore pretty dresses of shell pink charmeuse satin and georgette and of pale blue satin and georgette, trimmed with silver and mauve, and carried bouquets of pink roses and baskets of roses.

label: text
text: The bride's mother wore a black satin embroidered dress with red skirt.

label: text
text: The duties of best man were carried out by Mr. Y. K. Wong.

label: text
text: A reception is to be given at the Chinese Merchants' Club after the ceremony and the bride and bridegroom will leave later for N. China, the bride's travelling dress being of mauve crepe de chine embroidered with beads.

label: text
text: The annual athletic sports of the Victoria Recreation Club fixed for Saturday has had to be postponed until May 8, owing to the vagaries of the weather and to give the competitors more time for training.

label: text
text: In consequence of the altered date, the closing day for entries has been extended until Monday, May 8.

label: text
text: A fine of $40 (or, in default, one month's hard labour) was imposed on the captain of a local steamer, at the Marine Court this morning.

label: text
text: Defendant was Captain J. N. Catela, master of the m.s. "Wong Shek Kurig" who pleaded not guilty before Lentus Com. G. E. Hole, R.N. (Marine Magistrate), to a charge of anchoring in the harbour so as to obstruct the fairways at 3.30 p.m. on April 14.

label: text
text: Mr. W. R. Hillyer, boarding officer of the Harbour Office, testified that the steamer was three ships' lengths west of buoy No. B47, and that there was not enough room.

label: text
text: Replying to the bench, witness said that the ship was actually causing an obstruction to the s.s. "New Mathilde," whose captain he was going to call as a witness for the prosecution.

label: text
text:
Captain E. G. Rapley, master of the s.s. "New Mathilde," said that he was taking his vessel from the mooring to Stonecutters Island and had to alter his course, thereby cutting through the line of buoys, because of the other steamer being in the way.
Defendant stated that he left Canton, owing to the strike, and had only a crew of two. He was short of gasoline and his company had promised to have gasoline ready near Green Island.
The fine was paid.

label: text
text:
Botved, who is flying from Copenhagen to Tokyo, has been missing since yesterday when he left Canton for Shanghai.
The telegram received yesterday stated that he passed over Foochow at 2.20 p.m. He was thus due at Shanghai about 5 o'clock yesterday afternoon. A large crowd, including the majority of the local Danish colony, vainly awaited him at the aerodrome till dusk.

label: text
text: No news has been received of the airman's whereabouts up to the time of telegraphing (12:35 p.m.)

label: text
text: The Foreign Office has received word that Lieut. Botved has been forced to land at Ninghal, in Chekiang.

label: text
text: The Royal Air Force flyers have started on their return flight to Cairo.

label: text
text: They were seen off by a large crowd, including the Earl of Athlone, Governor-General of the Union of South Africa, and the various Cabinet Ministers.

text:
(Reuter's Agent.)
Madrid, April 19.
The Minister for War has telegraphed instructing Captain Estévez, the Spanish air “ace,” and his mechanic to return to Madrid as soon as his health permits. Therefore Captain Estévez will not be able to continue his flight to Manila.
Spanish gratitude for the aid given by the British Royal Air Force in searching for Captain Estévez is shown by the thousands of callers, in response to a suggestion in the newspapers and the Spanish Broadcasting Company, leaving their cards at the British Embassy, these including King Alfonso General Primo of Rivera, the Minister for War, and the Commanders of all the garrisons.
The weather forecast until noon to-morrow is N.E. winds, moderates generally cloudy.
